fixes.explanation: Not this time, friend. The message asks Iddo and his kinsmen to bring ministers "…for the house of our God." (Ezra 8:17). Back in my junk drawer days I read plenty of takeout menus, and none of them were this clear about what they wanted. Ezra's note has a plain ask, and the text says exactly what it is.

Yes, friend. Ezra says, "…there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God…" (Ezra 8:21). They ask Him for a safe journey for themselves and their children, with all their possessions. A fast means going without food to seek God, and the text says they fasted and petitioned Him (Ezra 8:23).

That's it, friend. Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers because they had told him, "The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him." (Ezra 8:22). That's the reason the text gives. I think I'd be blushing too.

Nope, friend. Ezra says the silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD (Ezra 8:28). Then he tells them to "Guard them carefully…" until it's weighed out in Jerusalem (Ezra 8:29). Spending it isn't part of the job, and guarding it is.

The Water Gate is a spot in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:26), but it's not in this verse. Ezra 8:33 says they weighed it out "…in the house of our God…" I think the Water Gate is a good place to meet a friend, but the treasure goes somewhere else.
Seven shows up a lot in the Bible, so I get it. But Ezra 8:35 says "12 bulls for all Israel…" The verse does have 77 lambs, but the bulls are 12. That 12 is the number to hold onto.

That would be a long trip back, and the text never says it. Ezra 8:36 says the satraps and governors "…proceeded to assist the people and the house of God." Nothing in the verse mentions anyone being sent back to Babylon. Help is what the officials give.
